sections.title: Executive investment summary: a Rs 156 crore Hyderabad contract assembler priced as a defence platform

subsections.title: What the company actually does, in plain terms

blocks.text: [F] Merritronix Limited is a business-to-business Electronics Systems Design and Manufacturing (ESDM) services provider making high-reliability, mission-critical electronic assemblies and systems for defence, aerospace, telecommunications and specialised industrial applications; its offering spans component sourcing, PCB assembly (SMT and THT), system integration, testing and box-build (PPT Jul 2026). [F] It was incorporated in October 1988 and is classified under Industrials > Capital Goods > Industrial Manufacturing (SCREENER). [F] Operations are run from a single disclosed address, C-22 Electronic Complex, Kushaiguda, Hyderabad, Telangana (PPT Jul 2026).

[F] It makes money through four disclosed revenue drivers: turnkey manufacturing (end-to-end execution including design support, sourcing, assembly, integration, testing and delivery); job work (customer supplies design and materials, the company assembles); obsolescence and engineering services (reverse engineering, form-fit-function replacement, selective redesign for legacy defence and aerospace platforms); and trading sales (procuring components from authorised global suppliers and supplying them directly to customers) (PPT Jul 2026). [E] Economically the profit pool is a mark-up on bought-in material: raw materials were 78.6% of FY26 revenue and employee cost plus other expenses together only 3.9%, so the EBITDA margin is almost exactly the gross material mark-up less a very thin overhead layer (PPT Jul 2026).

blocks.caption: End markets, geography and revenue scale as disclosed
rows: Aerospace and Defence share of revenue

blocks.text: [AI] Two facts on that table sit awkwardly together and frame the whole report: Aerospace and Defence is 97.81% of revenue, yet roughly 92% of revenue comes from non-government customers. The company is therefore overwhelmingly a sub-tier supplier into defence and aerospace supply chains run by private primes and intermediaries, not a direct prime contractor to the Ministry of Defence or to defence PSUs. [MC] Management's own stated strategy of 'Margin Expansion via Direct PSU Engagement' to reduce 'intermediary dependence' confirms that direct PSU work is today the exception rather than the rule (PPT Jul 2026).

[F] Customer profile is not disclosed in any usable form. No customer is named with a revenue number anywhere in the documents available to us; only two PSU approvals are named - Bharat Electronics Limited (approved supplier since 2009) and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (since 2012) - plus aerospace deliveries to Honeywell Aerospace (PPT Jul 2026). [F] Top-1, top-5 and top-10 customer concentration is not disclosed. [AI] For a company whose single largest analytical risk is customer concentration, this is the most important disclosure gap in the file.

[AI] Evidence-base warning. This report is written without four documents a deep dive would normally rest on. The FY2025-26 annual report was submitted to BSE on 7 September 2026 (ANNOUNCEMENTS) but is not in our evidence folder, so there is no auditor report, no key audit matters, no CARO annexure, no contingent liabilities note, no related-party schedule and no board composition. The IPO prospectus was not available, so there is no risk-factor section, no customer concentration table and no use-of-proceeds split. No earnings-call transcript exists or was available - the company listed only three months ago and the first analyst or investor meet was merely intimated on 15 September 2026 (ANNOUNCEMENTS). Consequently there is no management guidance of any kind to test in this report. Everything below is built from an investor presentation, a one-page credit bulletin, five announcement headlines and the statements data.

[F] A second consequence of the recent listing: the only quarterly data point in our statements data is the September 2025 quarter - Q2 FY26 - with sales of Rs 56 crore, EBITDA of Rs 8 crore, a 15% operating margin, PAT of Rs 4 crore and EPS of Rs 3.24 (NUMBERS). [E] For scale, the Q2 FY26 quarter alone was 35.9% of the full FY26 revenue, which implies material intra-year lumpiness that the absence of a quarterly series conceals.

subsections.title: Bear thesis: the strongest reasons not to own it

blocks.text: [AI] These are ordered by how much they would change a reasonable investor's mind, not by how easily they are dismissed.

items: **1. Profit has not become cash, and the gap is widening.** [F] Operating cash flow was minus Rs 23.38 cr in FY26 and minus Rs 6.64 cr in FY25 against reported PAT of Rs 16.10 cr and Rs 8.66 cr (PPT Jul 2026). [F] Cumulative operating cash flow over the last three years was minus 0.89 times reported profit, and cumulative free cash flow was minus Rs 31 cr (NUMBERS). [AI] Two consecutive years of negative operating cash flow during the company's best-ever profit growth is the single most important fact in this file.

**2. Growth is being bought with working capital at an unsustainable rate.** [E] Operating working capital (current assets excluding cash, less current liabilities excluding short-term borrowings) rose from Rs 11.96 cr in FY24 to Rs 29.59 cr in FY25 to Rs 65.33 cr in FY26, i.e. from 14.0% to 26.1% to 41.9% of revenue (PPT Jul 2026). [E] In FY26 the company consumed 84 paise of incremental working capital for every rupee of incremental revenue (Rs 35.74 cr against Rs 42.33 cr). [AI] At that conversion ratio, growth is self-defeating without permanent external funding.

**3. Inventory is the whole story and it is very large.** [F] Inventories were Rs 71.31 cr at 31 March 2026 against Rs 39.69 cr a year earlier (PPT Jul 2026). [E] That is 45.7% of full-year revenue and 58.2% of the full-year raw material cost. [F] Inventory days rose from 156 to 213 and the cash conversion cycle from 164 to 226 days (NUMBERS). [E] Inventory alone equals 72.7% of the entire disclosed order book of Rs 98.06 cr. [MC] Management's explanation is pre-emptive stocking of long-lead and critical components to ensure production continuity (PPT Jul 2026); there is no ageing schedule, no provisioning policy and no write-down disclosure to test it against.

**4. Concentration is worsening on every axis the company discloses, and is undisclosed on the axis that matters most.** [E] Aerospace and Defence went from 80.27% to 88.51% to 97.81% of revenue across FY24-FY26; [F] Telangana went from 88.85% to 98.19% (PPT Jul 2026). [F] Customer concentration - top 1, top 5, top 10 - is not disclosed anywhere. [AI] A single-state, single-vertical, single-facility revenue base with undisclosed customer concentration is a concentration profile that must be assumed worse than average until proven otherwise.

**5. The employee cost line cannot support the design-and-engineering narrative.** [F] Total employee benefits expense was Rs 2.34 cr in FY26, Rs 1.71 cr in FY25 and Rs 1.72 cr in FY24 (PPT Jul 2026). [E] That is 1.50% of FY26 revenue. [AI] A company positioning itself on design support, R&D-led system capability expansion, reverse engineering and selective redesign is spending Rs 2.34 crore a year on all its people combined. Either the engineering content is thinner than the narrative, or a material part of the workforce sits outside the employee-cost line in a way no document discloses. Headcount is not disclosed.

**6. Price is far above every fair value our model produces, under any of its scenarios.** [F] At Rs 380 the bear, base and bull DCF fair values are Rs 12.9, Rs 79.9 and Rs 147.7 per share respectively (NUMBERS). [F] The reverse DCF says today's price requires about 66% a year sales growth for five years against 19.8% in the base case (NUMBERS). [AI] The bull case is not the counterweight to the price here; the bull case is also 61% below it.

**7. The FY26 share capital and reserves movement cannot be reconciled from anything disclosed.** [F] Share capital rose from Rs 1.45 cr to Rs 12.78 cr and reserves from Rs 15.39 cr to Rs 40.34 cr in FY26 (PPT Jul 2026). [E] Reserves rose Rs 24.96 cr against PAT of Rs 16.10 cr - an Rs 8.86 cr excess - while share capital simultaneously rose by Rs 11.33 cr, a combination retained earnings cannot produce. [E] Financing cash inflow of Rs 41.15 cr against a Rs 24.63 cr rise in borrowings leaves roughly Rs 16.5 cr of non-debt financing inflow in FY26, before the June 2026 IPO. [F] No bonus ratio, no subdivision ratio, no pre-IPO allotment, no allottee and no issue price for any FY26 share issue is disclosed in any document available to us.

**8. The listed history is ten weeks long, the float is thin and the price has already traded in a near-70% band.** [F] Listed 8 June 2026; 52-week range Rs 283.10 to Rs 483.90 against a current Rs 380.04 (PPT Jul 2026). [F] 1,000 shareholders (NUMBERS). [AI] (BOARD) Our own earlier notes could not obtain daily traded value and treat the stock as sub-Rs 25-lakh-a-day liquidity until proven otherwise. Price discovery is not complete and position sizing is constrained by the exit, not the entry.

**9. The export narrative is contradicted by the export numbers.** [F] The presentation positions the company as 'Export-Ready' and cites exports to Europe, yet export revenue fell from Rs 1.10 cr (1.28% of revenue) in FY24 to Rs 1.27 cr (1.12%) in FY25 to Rs 0.57 cr (0.37%) in FY26 (PPT Jul 2026). [AI] Exports are shrinking in absolute terms in the company's best growth year.

**10. Debt is expensive, the tax rate is high, and neither is assumed away by our own model.** [E] FY26 finance costs of Rs 4.08 cr on average borrowings of about Rs 30.9 cr imply an effective cost of roughly 13.2% (PPT Jul 2026). [E] The effective tax rate was 30.05% in FY26 and 30.14% in FY25, against the 25.2% our DCF assumes (PPT Jul 2026, NUMBERS). [AI] The model is more generous on tax than the company's own history.

**11. Governance disclosure in the file is a family-executive list, not a board.** [F] The presentation names five people - the Managing Director, the Chairperson and Executive Director, an Executive Director who is also CFO, and two further promoters - with no ages, no appointment dates, no independent directors, no auditor name and no remuneration (PPT Jul 2026). [F] The Executive Director and CFO is described as having 'over 3 years of experience in finance and accounting' (PPT Jul 2026).

**12. The credit rating is referenced but never stated.** [F] Crisil's 17 June 2026 bulletin notes the IPO and says it is still in discussion with management and will take appropriate rating action after obtaining clarity; it does not state the rating symbol, outlook or rated amount (RATING). [AI] The document flags working-capital-intensive operations and margin susceptibility to input-price volatility as the offsetting weaknesses - the same two issues the financial statements show.

blocks.text: [AI] The market appears to be pricing Merritronix as an early-stage Indian defence-electronics platform, where the relevant variables are the size of the indigenisation opportunity and the scarcity of qualified suppliers. The evidence in this file supports a narrower description: a 38-year-old, single-facility, single-state contract assembler with genuine and hard-won aerospace and defence qualifications, whose profit is a mark-up on bought-in material, whose overhead base is too small to generate operating leverage, and whose entire recent growth has been financed by inventory, supplier-independent debt and, since June 2026, IPO equity. The variant perception is not that the business is bad - a 34.8% revenue CAGR with 8.8 points of gross margin expansion is a genuinely good two years - but that the distance between Rs 380 and the Rs 79.9 base-case fair value is not an argument about assumptions. Our base case already embeds 30% starting growth and a 19.8% five-year-equivalent CAGR; the price needs 66%. That is a scale gap, not an assumption gap, and no disclosure in this file closes it.

subsections.title: What the timeline actually reveals about how new the current business is

blocks.text: [AI] The 1988 incorporation date is doing a lot of work in the narrative and rather less in the numbers. The company spent its first fifteen to twenty years in telecom cable jointing kits, entered defence and aerospace only in 2007, earned its first PSU approval in 2009 and its second in 2012, and added high-density PCB capability in 2017. So the current business - Aerospace and Defence at 97.81% of revenue - is at most a nineteen-year-old business and, on the revenue evidence, a much more recent one than that: [E] Aerospace and Defence was 80.27% of revenue as recently as FY24 and the company's revenue base has nearly doubled since. [F] Three quarters of the revenue that exists today did not exist three years ago: FY24 revenue was Rs 85.70 cr against Rs 155.90 cr in FY26 (PPT Jul 2026).

[AI] The correct way to read the 37-year history is as an explanation of why the qualifications exist, not as evidence of execution durability at the current scale. The company has never before operated at Rs 156 crore of revenue, never before carried Rs 71 crore of inventory, never before been a listed entity with quarterly reporting obligations, and has had a public share price for ten weeks. The oldest thing about the business is the relationships; the newest thing is everything an investor is being asked to pay for.

blocks.text: [F] The disclosed chain, in order, is: component sourcing from authorised global suppliers; PCB assembly by surface-mount (SMT) and through-hole (THT) technology; system integration; testing and inspection; box-build and electromechanical assembly; and finished-product delivery (PPT Jul 2026). [F] Around this core the company adds design support at the front end for turnkey work, and obsolescence management at the back end - reverse engineering, form-fit-function replacement, alternate component qualification and selective redesign for legacy platforms (PPT Jul 2026).

[F] Step 2 - Assembly. SMT and THT lines handle high-density, high-complexity assemblies including BGA and micro-BGA components (PPT Jul 2026).
[F] Step 3 - Inspection and test. Automated optical inspection, X-ray inspection and functional testing, under IPC-A-610 Class 3 compliant processes (PPT Jul 2026).
[F] Step 4 - Integration and box build. System integration and box-build solutions delivering ready-to-deploy systems (PPT Jul 2026).
[F] Step 5 - Lifecycle support. Obsolescence management extending the operational life of fielded platforms without full replacement (PPT Jul 2026).

[F] A parallel track sits outside this chain entirely: trading sales, in which components are procured and supplied directly to customers without passing through assembly (PPT Jul 2026). [AI] This is a distribution activity recorded inside manufacturing revenue.

subsections.title: Where value is captured, and why

blocks.text: [E] The value capture arithmetic is unusually transparent because the cost structure has only three lines. On FY26 revenue of Rs 155.90 cr: raw materials Rs 122.58 cr (78.63%), employee benefits Rs 2.34 cr (1.50%), other expenses Rs 3.75 cr (2.41%), leaving EBITDA of Rs 27.22 cr (17.46%) before other income (PPT Jul 2026). [AI] Value is therefore captured almost entirely in the spread between what components cost and what the assembled product sells for, and that spread is protected by qualification status rather than by cost advantage, scale, brand or intellectual property.

[AI] The critical implication is that there is no operating-leverage engine. With fixed overheads of under 4% of revenue, incremental revenue at constant gross margin drops through at roughly the gross margin, not at a multiple of it. [E] This is visible in the data: FY26 gross margin proxy rose 2.98 points (18.39% to 21.37%) and EBITDA margin rose 4.11 points (13.31% to 17.42%), so slightly more than the gross-margin gain flowed through, helped by other expenses falling from 3.55% to 2.41% of revenue (PPT Jul 2026). [AI] The corollary is that margin is fragile in the other direction too: a gross-margin reversal is an EBITDA reversal with nothing to absorb it.

[AI] Value capture and cash capture are different things here. FY26 captured Rs 27.22 cr of EBITDA and Rs 16.10 cr of PAT, and simultaneously handed Rs 35.74 cr back to working capital [E]. The economics of a rupee of Merritronix revenue are good on the income statement and, so far, negative in cash.

blocks.text: [F] Our statements data reports working capital days of 64 for FY26, up from 51 in FY25 and 9 in FY24 (NUMBERS). [AI] Taken alone that reads as a manageable deterioration. It is not, and the reason is definitional: a screener-style working capital days figure is computed on a net basis that includes short-term borrowings and cash within current liabilities and current assets, so a company that funds its inventory with a bank overdraft appears to have less working capital, not more. **The same year in which working capital days rose 13 days saw operating cash flow fall by Rs 16.74 cr.** Those two facts cannot both be the headline.

[E] Rebuilt on an operating basis - current assets excluding cash, less current liabilities excluding short-term borrowings - operating working capital was Rs 11.96 cr in FY24, Rs 29.59 cr in FY25 and Rs 65.33 cr in FY26, or 14.0%, 26.1% and 41.9% of revenue (PPT Jul 2026). [AI] That is the figure an owner funds, and it has tripled as a share of revenue in two years. The cash conversion cycle in our statements data tells the same story with less ambiguity: 19 days in FY24, 164 in FY25, 226 in FY26 (NUMBERS).

The credit bulletin names no peer and provides no industry comparison (RATING). The company profile contains none (SCREENER). The announcements contain none. A listed-peer comparison table is a standard feature of both an Indian IPO prospectus and most investor presentations; its complete absence here means this section cannot be populated with data and must instead explain the consequences.

subsections.title: Competitors named by management, and what they really are

blocks.text: [F] Management names no competitor anywhere. The word does not appear in the presentation in any company-specific form. [F] The closest the company comes to competitive positioning is the industry-overview claim that 'EMS providers with capabilities in precision manufacturing, system integration, compliance, testing and lifecycle support are better placed to capture premium margins' (PPT Jul 2026) - a statement about a category, not about rivals.

[AI] What the company does instead is describe barriers and then imply it is on the right side of them: EN 9100:2018 certification, IPC-A-610 Class 3 processes, BGA and micro-BGA capability with X-ray validation, approved-supplier status at BEL and HAL, and NADCAP discussions initiated (PPT Jul 2026). [AI] That is a defensible way to position a company that genuinely cannot name its competitors - in defence sub-tier supply, competitor identity is often commercially sensitive. But an investor should register what is being lost: without a peer set, there is no way to know whether a 17.42% EBITDA margin is good or ordinary for this work, whether 213 inventory days is a company problem or an industry norm, whether 86 debtor days is tight or loose, or whether the company is gaining or losing share.

[AI] We deliberately do not construct a peer set from memory. Naming Indian listed EMS or defence-electronics companies and attaching revenue, margin or multiple figures to them would be exactly the fabrication these evidence rules exist to prevent, since no such data exists in this folder. The correct analytical output here is the gap itself, plus its consequences, which are set out below.

items: [AI] **Consequence 1 - the margin cannot be benchmarked.** The bull case rests on a gross margin that rose from 12.58% to 21.37% [E]. Without peer margins there is no way to judge whether 21.37% is a defensible structural level for defence-qualified EMS work or an unusually good two years. Our DCF's 13% base-case assumption exists precisely because that question cannot be answered from evidence (NUMBERS).

[AI] **Consequence 2 - share gain cannot be verified.** [E] The company grew revenue at a 34.80% CAGR while the EMS market it cites grew at an implied ~9.6% CAGR to 2031 (PPT Jul 2026). That looks like share gain, but a company at roughly 0.04-0.05% of the cited market can grow at any rate for years without share dynamics being the explanation - winning two customers would do it.

[AI] **Consequence 3 - the moat cannot be tested against substitutes.** Approved-supplier status at BEL and HAL is valuable only in proportion to how few other suppliers hold it. That number is not disclosed and cannot be inferred.

[AI] **Consequence 4 - pricing pressure is invisible until it arrives.** With no competitor data and no disclosed contract terms, the first evidence of competitive pressure will be a margin decline already reported, not a leading indicator.

[F] **Consequence 5 - the only external competitive read in the file is Crisil's**, and it is generic: extensive promoter experience in the EMS industry and a comfortable financial risk profile, partially offset by working-capital-intensive operations and margin susceptibility to input prices (RATING). [AI] Crisil does not position the company against peers either.

[AI] Net assessment: the competitive position is **asserted rather than demonstrated**. The credentials are real and verifiable; the competitive standing those credentials confer is not disclosed, not benchmarked and not assessable from this file.

subsections.title: The two questions the scores cannot answer

blocks.text: [AI] **Question one: how many other companies hold the same approvals?** The entire moat rests on scarcity of qualification. If BEL and HAL have approved forty suppliers for comparable sub-assemblies, the approval is a licence to compete rather than a barrier. If they have approved four, it is a genuine franchise. The company does not disclose this, no peer data exists in the file, and the difference between those two worlds is the difference between a score of 8 and a score of 3 on the most heavily weighted factor. [AI] The circumstantial evidence cuts both ways: 14-17 year relationships suggest the position is defensible, while roughly 92% of revenue coming from non-government intermediaries suggests the PSU approvals are not where most of the business actually sits.

[AI] **Question two: does the moat survive at the customer's option or at the company's?** Switching costs protect an incumbent only until the customer decides the cost is worth paying - and in EMS the customer usually retains the design, the specification and often the component sourcing. [F] No long-term agreement, minimum volume, exclusivity (other than the June 2026 Stuam MoU, whose terms are undisclosed) or price-escalation mechanism is disclosed for any customer relationship. [AI] A moat that exists entirely in the customer's inconvenience is real but asymmetric: it prevents casual switching, not determined switching, and it confers very little pricing power in a renegotiation.

[AI] There is a moat, it is narrow, and it is the right kind of narrow. **The defensible asset is qualification status plus platform knowledge; everything else on the scorecard is close to zero.** That combination - high approval barriers, high switching costs, no scale, no IP, no input control, no network effects - is the standard profile of a qualified niche supplier. It supports above-commodity margins and long customer lives; it does not support pricing power, share gains against determined competition, or protection from input-cost inflation.

[AI] The practically important conclusion for valuation is this: a 4.1 out of 10 moat can justify a durable business, but it cannot justify the growth persistence that the price requires. Moats of this type protect the revenue a company already has far better than they help it win revenue it does not have. Our reverse DCF requires about 66% annual sales growth for five years (NUMBERS); nothing on this scorecard is a mechanism for delivering that. The qualification moat is a reason the business should survive, not a reason it should compound.

blocks.text: [AI] Note what the bull case actually asks for and what it delivers. It asks for sales to more than triple to Rs 531.7 cr by FY31, at a 15% EBITDA margin - a genuinely demanding operating outcome requiring roughly Rs 376 cr of additional revenue from a business with one factory and an unnamed customer base. [F] It delivers Rs 147.7 per share, 61.1% below the current price (NUMBERS). [AI] **The bull case is not an argument for the shares at Rs 380; it is a demonstration that even a demanding operating outcome does not reach the price.**

[AI] We decline to attach numerical probabilities, because the evidence base does not support them: with one quarterly datapoint, no guidance, no customer disclosure, no peer set, no post-listing results and no annual report, any probability distribution would be a manufactured precision. items: [AI] The **bear case's growth assumption (12% fading to 5%) looks too pessimistic against the evidence**: the company grew 37.3% in FY26, holds a Rs 98.06 cr order book and has capacity headroom. Its margin assumption of 9.0% is, however, entirely achievable - [E] a 10% input-cost increase absorbed without pass-through would take the FY26 margin to 9.60%.

[AI] The **base case's growth assumption looks reasonable for one to two years and increasingly demanding thereafter**, because the constraint is working capital funding rather than demand. [E] Base-case sales of Rs 384.8 cr by FY31 would require roughly Rs 190 cr of incremental working capital at FY26's conversion ratio, against Rs 70.03 cr of IPO proceeds.

[AI] The **base case's margin assumption of 13.0% looks too pessimistic against two years of delivered evidence**, and is the assumption most likely to be revised upward as post-listing results accumulate. This is the strongest single argument a bull can make about the model.
[AI] The **bull case's combination is internally coherent but operationally very demanding**, and it still lands 61.1% below the price.

[AI] The distribution that matters is therefore not bear-versus-bull; it is that **all three scenarios sit far below the current price**, with a spread of Rs 12.9 to Rs 147.7 against Rs 380. An investor's real question is not which scenario is right but what would have to be true outside all three of them.

blocks.text: [F] **There is no disclosed peer set.** No peer comparison, benchmarking table or competitor multiple appears in the investor presentation, the credit bulletin, the company profile or the announcements. We therefore cannot compare 41.6x earnings, 26.2x EV/EBITDA or 4.54x EV/sales against anything, and we decline to construct a peer group from outside the evidence base. This is a genuine analytical limitation and it is the company's disclosure gap, not an oversight in this report.

[AI] What can be said without a peer set is how the multiples relate to the company's own fundamentals. [E] At 4.54x EV/sales the market is capitalising a business with a 17.42% EBITDA margin, a 78.63% material cost base and negative operating cash flow. At 26.2x EV/EBITDA it is capitalising Rs 27 cr of EBITDA that converted into minus Rs 23 cr of operating cash flow. At 41.6x earnings it is capitalising Rs 16 cr of profit that has never been collected in cash. [AI] The multiples are not extreme by the standards of Indian small-cap defence-adjacent names; what is unusual is the cash profile underneath them.

[AI] One adjustment an investor should make mentally, and which our valuation data flags but does not apply: the enterprise value of Rs 708 cr is gross of Rs 25.70 cr of disclosed March-2026 cash and takes no account of the Rs 70.03 cr raised in June 2026 (NUMBERS, PPT Jul 2026, RATING). [AI] Both the EV-based multiples and the DCF equity bridge are therefore computed against a balance sheet that materially predates the company's current financial position. We do not restate them, because restating them would create valuation figures that do not exist in our model, but the direction of the error is knowable: the EV multiples are overstated and the DCF per-share values are understated.

[F] Our DCF is flagged as both available and meaningful, and produces bear, base and bull equity values of Rs 12.9, Rs 79.9 and Rs 147.7 per share, against a price of Rs 380 - implied changes of -96.6%, -79.0% and -61.1% respectively (NUMBERS). [AI] A gap of this size between a mechanical DCF and a market price is worth interrogating rather than simply reporting, and there are three honest interpretations that an investor should weigh together.

items: [AI] **Interpretation 1 - the model's operating assumptions are too harsh.** The base case uses a 13.0% EBITDA margin against 17.42% delivered, and caps starting growth at 30% against 43.3% realised over three years. A margin assumption that low, applied across five explicit years and the terminal value, is the single largest source of the gap. This is a legitimate and substantial criticism.

[AI] **Interpretation 2 - the model's balance sheet is out of date.** It deducts Rs 43 cr of borrowings and adds neither the Rs 25.70 cr of March-2026 cash nor the Rs 70.03 cr of June-2026 IPO proceeds. Both omissions push the per-share values down.

[AI] **Interpretation 3 - the price embeds expectations the model is not designed to capture.** A newly listed, thinly held defence-adjacent SME with a well-publicised backer trades on scarcity, narrative and float dynamics as much as on discounted cash flow. Our own earlier notes record roughly 1,000 shareholders, a near-70% price band since listing and no brokerage coverage (BOARD, NUMBERS).

[AI] All three can be true simultaneously and they still do not close a Rs 380-versus-Rs 147.7 gap. Correcting interpretations 1 and 2 in the bull's favour moves the fair value; it does not move it fourfold. The residual, whatever its size, is interpretation 3.

blocks.text: [AI] A necessary caution on the DCF itself: 78.7% of base-case enterprise value is terminal value [E], the model uses a single beta of 1.15 with no illiquidity or concentration adjustment, and it assumes working capital days of 41.3 in a business running a 226-day cash conversion cycle. [F] Our statements data raises this as a red-level flag in its own right: 'Price needs growth well above trend - today's price implies about 66% a year sales growth for five years, against 20% in the base case' (NUMBERS). [AI] The forensic conclusion follows from combining that with the cash evidence. To grow sales at 66% a year the company would need to fund working capital at, on FY26's ratio, roughly 84 paise per incremental rupee of revenue [E] - which on a twelve-fold revenue increase is an amount of capital vastly exceeding the Rs 70.03 crore raised, the Rs 43.20 cr of existing borrowings and any plausible internal generation. **The growth the price requires is not merely operationally demanding; it is financially incompatible with the company's demonstrated cash conversion.** Either the working capital intensity collapses, or the growth cannot be funded, or the equity is diluted repeatedly. The reverse DCF and the cash flow statement are, in this case, the same finding stated two ways.
[AI] Intellectual honesty requires putting the bull's best case against the above as forcefully as possible, and it is not weak.

items: [AI] **The reverse DCF inherits every one of the base model's assumptions, including the 13.0% EBITDA margin.** Run at the 17.42% margin the company actually delivered, the growth rate required to justify the price would be materially lower than 66%. We do not compute how much lower, because that would create a valuation figure not present in our model - but the direction is unambiguous and the effect is large, because margin scales the entire cash flow stream.

[AI] **It also inherits the balance-sheet omissions.** The enterprise value it solves against is Rs 708 cr, gross of Rs 25.70 cr of March-2026 cash and taking no account of Rs 70.03 cr of June-2026 IPO proceeds (NUMBERS, PPT Jul 2026, RATING). Both push the required growth rate down.

[AI] **The working-capital constraint may be a stage, not a structure.** [F] The company describes its inventory as pre-emptive stocking of long-lead components (PPT Jul 2026), and a supplier building a position ahead of programme ramp genuinely does carry stock before it carries revenue. If inventory days revert toward FY25's 156 from 213, a substantial cash release follows with no new customers required (NUMBERS).

[AI] **The market may be pricing something the model structurally cannot see**: optionality on the Stuam exclusive manufacturing relationship, on NADCAP accreditation, on direct PSU conversion, on India's defence indigenisation capex cycle, and on a qualified supplier's scarcity value. A DCF fed on trailing financials values none of these, by construction.

[AI] **And the mechanical caveat**: a 66% required CAGR is the output of a model whose terminal value is 78.7% of enterprise value [E]. Reverse DCFs on early-stage, high-growth companies routinely produce implausible-looking required rates that later prove achievable for a few years - the arithmetic is unforgiving of a low starting base.

blocks.text: [AI] Weighing both sides: the counter-arguments are real and they would move the required growth rate meaningfully, but they operate on the margin assumption and the balance-sheet bridge, not on the fundamental shape of the finding. **The gap between what the price requires and what the company has demonstrated is measured in multiples, not percentages, and no adjustment available within this evidence base closes it.** That is the single most important conclusion in this report, and it is stated as a fact about the arithmetic, not as a recommendation.

subsections.title: Where the price sits against value, and what drives the gap

blocks.text: [F] Merritronix trades at Rs 380 per share and Rs 665 crore of market capitalisation, against modelled fair values of Rs 12.9 (bear), Rs 79.9 (base) and Rs 147.7 (bull), on 41.6x trailing earnings, 26.2x EV/EBITDA and 4.54x EV/sales (NUMBERS). [F] The reverse DCF implies the price requires about 66% annual sales growth for five years, against a base-case equivalent of 19.8% and a realised three-year rate of 43.3% (NUMBERS). [AI] **This report expresses no buy, sell or hold view and sets no price target.** What it can state is the arithmetic: the price sits above the top of our modelled range by a multiple, not a margin, and no point in the sensitivity grid reaches it.

[AI] Four things drive the gap, and an investor should be clear about which they believe. **One, the model's margin assumption.** Base case 13.0% and bull case 15.0% against 17.42% delivered - a real and legitimate criticism that moves the fair value up meaningfully. **Two, the model's stale balance sheet.** Rs 25.70 cr of March-2026 cash is not netted and Rs 70.03 cr of June-2026 IPO proceeds are not added; both understate per-share value. **Three, optionality the model cannot see** - the Stuam exclusive arrangement, NADCAP, direct PSU conversion, unused SMT capacity. **Four, and residually, market factors**: a three-month-old BSE SME listing with 1,000 shareholders, a 71% price band, no brokerage coverage and, per our own earlier notes, a well-publicised backer (BOARD, NUMBERS, PPT Jul 2026).

[AI] The honest apportionment is that the first three factors are real and would move a fair value materially - they are why this report does not treat Rs 79.9 as a target. They are not, in combination, capable of explaining a fourfold gap. The residual is the fourth factor, and an investor buying here should know that is what they are buying.

items: [AI] This is not a company that can be underwritten on a quarter. The thesis rests on whether working capital intensity is a growth-stage feature or a structural one, and that question needs at least four quarters of post-listing data to answer. [F] At present there is not one post-listing quarterly result in this evidence base.

[AI] The minimum evidence set before any position is sized: the FY2025-26 annual report (filed 7 September 2026), the IPO prospectus, and two consecutive post-listing quarters with balance sheets. Without the first two, the customer concentration, related-party, contingent liability, pledge and lock-in questions are simply unanswerable.

[AI] The appropriate horizon for the operating thesis is three to five years, because the qualification-based moat protects revenue over long periods but produces its returns slowly, and because the capacity and mix levers available today take years to show in the numbers.

[AI] The appropriate horizon for the valuation question is much shorter, and it is uncomfortable: at 41.6x trailing earnings on a company with negative free cash flow, the valuation is being carried by sentiment that can reprice in weeks, in a stock whose 52-week band is already 71% wide.

[AI] Position-sizing constraint, stated separately from the thesis: [F] 1,000 shareholders on a BSE SME platform (NUMBERS), with our own earlier notes unable to establish daily traded value and treating liquidity as sub-Rs 25 lakh a day until proven otherwise (BOARD). Exit capacity, not entry conviction, is the binding constraint here.

[F] No previous report exists for Merritronix Limited in our research base, so this is initial coverage and there is no prior quarter's numbers, disclosures, guidance delivery, risks or thesis to compare against. summary.one_line: Merritronix is a genuinely qualified, fast-growing but cash-consuming defence-and-aerospace contract assembler whose operating record is better than its cash statement and whose Rs 380 share price sits above every scenario in our DCF, including the bull case at Rs 147.7.
bull_points: Growth with margin expansion, delivered: revenue compounded 34.80% over FY24-FY26 to Rs 155.90 cr while EBITDA margin rose from 7.82% to 17.42% and PAT from Rs 3.05 cr to Rs 16.10 cr [F] (PPT Jul 2026); 8.79 points of that came from the gross-material line rather than cost-cutting [E] (PPT Jul 2026).

Real, dated qualification barriers that take years to earn: EN 9100:2018 certification, IPC-A-610 Class 3 processes, approved supplier to Bharat Electronics since 2009 and to Hindustan Aeronautics since 2012, CERN vendor via TIFR, with executed programmes including infrared seeker assemblies, airborne radar assemblies and defence-aircraft DVRS [F] (PPT Jul 2026).

The funding constraint was relieved right after the balance-sheet date: Rs 70.03 cr of primary IPO capital raised in June 2026 for capex, debt repayment, working capital and general corporate purposes [F] (RATING) - roughly three times the FY26 operating cash outflow, and absent from the 31 March 2026 balance sheet investors can see [F] (PPT Jul 2026).

Free capacity heading into FY27: the Panasonic NPM D3A line commissioned January 2026 lifted SMD capacity from 7,65,000 to 10,75,000 units and contributed zero production in April-December 2025, so volume growth needs no new capex [F] (PPT Jul 2026).

Fixed-asset efficiency is exceptional and leverage is falling: fixed asset turnover 26.0x, ROCE 41%, capex only 1.9% of sales [F] (NUMBERS), with debt-to-equity improving from 1.93x to 0.81x and interest cover from 3.0x to 6.8x over FY24-FY26 [F] (PPT Jul 2026, NUMBERS).
bear_points: Profit does not become cash and the gap widens every year: CFO/PAT of 1.67x, -0.78x and -1.44x across FY24-FY26, a three-year cumulative of -0.89x and three-year free cash flow of -Rs 31 cr [F] (NUMBERS); Rs 27.81 cr of cumulative profit produced -Rs 25.49 cr of cumulative operating cash flow [E] (PPT Jul 2026).

Growth is bought with working capital at an unsustainable rate: operating working capital rose from 14.0% to 41.9% of revenue in two years and FY26 consumed 84 paise of incremental working capital per incremental revenue rupee; the cash conversion cycle went from 19 days to 226 days [E]/[F] (PPT Jul 2026, NUMBERS). Inventory of Rs 71.31 cr is 45.7% of annual revenue and 72.7% of the entire disclosed order book [E] (PPT Jul 2026).

The price is above every modelled scenario: Rs 380 against bear Rs 12.9, base Rs 79.9 and bull Rs 147.7 per share, and the reverse DCF implies about 66% annual sales growth for five years against 19.8% in the base case [F] (NUMBERS). No corner of the sensitivity grid, which spans Rs 58.5 to Rs 117.4, reaches the price [F] (NUMBERS).

Concentration worsens on every disclosed axis and the most important one is undisclosed: Aerospace and Defence went from 80.27% to 97.81% of revenue and Telangana from 88.85% to 98.19%, with non-defence revenue falling 79.8% in absolute terms [E]/[F] (PPT Jul 2026), while top-1, top-5 and top-10 customer concentration is not disclosed anywhere [F].

The forensic evidence base has holes in exactly the wrong places: no annual report (filed with BSE on 7 September 2026 but unavailable to us), no IPO prospectus and no earnings-call transcript [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS) - so the auditor's opinion, CARO observations, contingent liabilities, related-party transactions, promoter pledges, lock-in expiry dates and board composition are all unknown, and no independent director or auditor is named in any document [F] (PPT Jul 2026).

The FY26 equity movement cannot be reconciled: reserves rose Rs 24.96 cr against PAT of Rs 16.10 cr while share capital rose Rs 11.33 cr, leaving roughly Rs 16.5 cr of non-debt financing inflow and, on the company's own per-share data, about 18.9 lakh shares issued during FY26 that no document describes [E] (PPT Jul 2026).
watch_points: Operating cash flow direction in the first post-listing half-year: the company has never in five years of record grown revenue and generated positive operating cash flow in the same year; FY26 CFO was -Rs 23.38 cr [F] (PPT Jul 2026). This single line settles the central debate.

Inventory days and the cash conversion cycle: 213 days and 226 days respectively at FY26, both multi-year worsts [F] (NUMBERS). Falling days alongside revenue growth would confirm the pre-emptive-stocking explanation; rising days would refute it.

The second order-book observation and its definition: Rs 98.06 cr as of 30 June 2026 is currently a single point with no definition, execution period or comparative, equal to a 0.63x book-to-bill [F]/[E] (PPT Jul 2026).
Utilisation of the Rs 70.03 cr IPO proceeds against the four stated objects, and whether short-term borrowings of Rs 37.90 cr are actually repaid [F] (RATING, PPT Jul 2026).

Three dated disclosure events that will resolve most open questions: the FY2025-26 annual report filed 7 September 2026, the AGM of 30 September 2026 including the MD remuneration revision approved on 3 September, and the Analyst / Investor Meet intimated 15 September 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS); plus the Crisil rating action open since 17 June 2026 [F] (RATING).
guidance: No quantified forward guidance of any kind was issued this period. No revenue, margin, order-book, capex, utilisation, product-launch or timeline target appears in the investor presentation, the credit bulletin or the exchange announcements [F] (PPT Jul 2026, RATING, ANNOUNCEMENTS). The items below are the forward-dated disclosures and qualitative commitments to carry into the next quarter's tracker; none of them is guidance.
Order book: 'Rs 98.06 crore Order book (as of June 30, 2026)' - stated without definition, customer split, product split or execution period [F] (PPT Jul 2026).
Repeat customer rate: '86.08%' as of 31 March 2026 - the metric's definition, numerator and denominator are not disclosed [MC] (PPT Jul 2026).

Installed capacity: '~2.095 million units annual installed capacity (FY2026)', being SMD 10.75 lakh, TMD 6.00 lakh and box build 4.20 lakh units, with SMD raised from 7,65,000 to 10,75,000 by the Panasonic NPM D3A commissioned January 2026, which 'contributed zero production during the April-December 2025 window' [F] (PPT Jul 2026).
Utilisation: 'Peak up to 99% Utilisation Achieved (TMD Section, FY26)'; expansion described as 'Demand-led Expansion' [F] (PPT Jul 2026).

Margin strategy: 'Margin Expansion via Direct PSU Engagement' - 'Direct engagement with defence PSUs reduces intermediary dependence'; 'Value-added capabilities enable execution of higher-complexity, higher-margin programs'; 'Reflected in sustained improvement in operating margins'. No target margin [MC] (PPT Jul 2026).
R&D: 'Invest in R&D to evolve from component-level work to complete system design and manufacturing'. No spend figure, no timeline [MC] (PPT Jul 2026).

Diversification: 'Selective expansion into adjacent high-reliability electronics platforms while defence and aerospace remain core... across UAVs, EV power electronics and advanced industrial applications', with 'limited incremental investment'. No revenue expectation, no date [MC] (PPT Jul 2026).

International: 'Build international revenues by entering regulated markets aligned with the Company's quality and execution capabilities'. No target; exports were 0.37% of FY26 revenue [MC]/[F] (PPT Jul 2026).
Capex: 'ongoing investments in advanced SMT, testing and inspection capabilities' and 'targeted automation and process improvements'. No amount, no timeline [MC] (PPT Jul 2026).

Certification: NADCAP certification 'discussions initiated' to align with global aerospace and defence quality standards - first referenced in the 2020-2022 timeline entry and still not completed as at July 2026 [F] (PPT Jul 2026).

Partnerships: MoU with Analinear Design Technologies Pvt Ltd as 'Preferred Manufacturing Partner' and an 'Exclusive Manufacturing Partnership' MoU with Stuam Technologies Limited naming the company 'preferred contract manufacturer for Stuam's current and future product portfolio', both June 2026, neither with any disclosed value, volume, term or minimum commitment [F] (PPT Jul 2026).

IPO proceeds: approximately Rs 70.03 crore raised via primary issue 'which shall be utilised for capital expenditure, repayment of part of debt, working capital requirements and general corporate purpose'; the split between the four uses is not disclosed [F] (RATING).

Credit rating: Crisil 'is in discussion with the company's management regarding this event and has also sought additional information', and 'will take appropriate rating action after getting clarity on these aspects'; the rating symbol, outlook and rated amount are not stated in the document available to us [F] (RATING).

Board and corporate actions: board meeting of 3 September 2026 approved an AGM on 30 September 2026, auditor appointments, an MD remuneration revision, and a further item recorded only as 'Rs 7' in the truncated announcement text, which cannot be identified; an Analyst / Investor Meet was intimated on 15 September 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS).
